records.name: Morelos
records.current_summary: No Morelos-specific statutes, bans or lethality placements are supported by the vetted sources for this map. The national picture governs: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six state legislatures enacting none; a March 2024 report documents that where no procedure exists, trans people face police stops, denied documents and institutional mistreatment.  Transfeminicide has become a criminal category in some states — the capital imposes up to 70 years — against more than 95% homicide impunity nationally, and reporting finds convictions lag the statutes. For a visitor, Morelos' own documented record is thin: expect the country-wide picture rather than verified local protections or verified local hostility.

sources.claim: National framework (HRW, 31 Mar 2025): legal gender recognition in Mexico is set state-by-state — as of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more run one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted none, and only seven states extend recognition to children. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022; the Inter-American Court likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. HRW documents the consequences where no procedure exists (identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco). For this record: the national mosaic, not any locally enacted certainty, is the operative framework.

HRW/Community Center for Inclusion report (6 Mar 2024) on a Mexican state lacking a legal gender-recognition procedure, documented in Tabasco: without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries violence, harassment and humiliation risk, excluding trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions; context includes the Aug 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and more than 95% of homicides nationally going unpunished in 2022. For this record it is the operative evidence of what 'state law silent' means for trans people on the ground.

flags: the 2024 national report grouped Morelos just behind Nuevo León in recorded killings of LGBT+ people

records.name: Nayarit
records.current_summary: Nayarit was the first of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfeminicide, introducing sentences of up to 60 years in early 2024 — a step the capital followed in July 2024 with its 70-year 'Paola Buenrostro law', named for a trans sex worker murdered in 2016 whose attacker was released after 48 hours despite footage and witnesses and has not been caught since. Nayarit's law also lets friends, not only relatives, claim bodies and drive investigations, which matters where families disown trans relatives.  That statute landed against more than 95% impunity for homicides in Mexico in 2022, believed higher for transfeminicides, so it records official posture more than proven protection. No other Nayarit-specific incidents or enforcement records are supported by the vetted sources; the national picture otherwise governs — by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six enacting none.

sources.claim: Nayarit-specific entry: a 2017 reform of the state Civil Code established an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, allowing adults to change identity documents to match gender identity. The 31 Mar 2025 national roundup counts 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated such procedures, EIGHT with none and two more practice-not-law (the record's 'six states' wording should read eight). The document also records the 2019 national Supreme Court guidelines and that only seven states extend recognition to children.

Names Nayarit as the FIRST of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfemicide, introducing sentences of up to 60 years earlier in 2024; Mexico City followed in July 2024 as the second, with up to 70 years (Paola Buenrostro law). The law also lets friends - not just relatives - identify and claim bodies and drive investigations, relevant where families disown trans relatives. Context: in 2022 more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished, the figure believed higher for transfemicides.

flags: Press reviews find such statutes have produced few convictions

records.name: Sonora
records.current_summary: No Sonora-specific laws, incidents or enforcement patterns are supported by the vetted sources for this map, and the claim that it sits outside the documented problem categories cannot itself be verified from them. The national picture governs: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six state legislatures enacting none; a March 2024 report documents that where no procedure exists, trans people face police stops, denied documents and institutional mistreatment.  Transfeminicide has become a criminal category in some states — the capital imposes up to 70 years — against more than 95% homicide impunity nationally, and reporting finds convictions lag the statutes. For a visitor, Sonora's own documented record is thin: expect the country-wide picture rather than verified local protections or verified local hostility.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time; the underlying source is a Human Rights Watch country overview (31 March 2025) on transgender rights progress and challenges in Mexico, headlining that 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and naming six whose legislatures had enacted none.

The page's state-by-state coverage names Sonora as one of the 25 Mexican states that have legislated a gender identity law, with Sonora dated to 2020, giving trans people a statutory procedure to rectify gender on civil documents. It further records that Sonora's Congress banned conversion therapies (ECOSIG) on 6 December 2022, and that Sonora is among the states whose hate-crime laws recognize motivation by gender and sexual preference and which ratified the 2011 constitutional amendment prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. On marriage, the page records that by 31 December 2022 every Mexican state, including Sonora, had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling. For this record: concrete Sonora-specific legal protections (gender-recognition procedure, conversion-therapy ban, hate-crime framework, marriage availability) that the current summary said were unsupported by vetted sources.

Hermosillo-based daily El Sol de Hermosillo (article dated 1 October 2020) reports that Sonora's Congress approved the state's Gender Identity Law ("Ley de Identidad de Género"), under which people who identify with the opposite gender can modify their official documentation. For this record: local-news confirmation that Sonora legislated a gender-recognition procedure for trans people in 2020, the state-level fact the country dossier currently lacks, and one of the procedures counted in the report that 22 of Mexico's 32 states have enacted such laws.

records.name: Tabasco
records.current_summary: Tabasco has enacted no legal procedure for recognising gender identity. A Human Rights Watch report co-produced with a local inclusion centre (March 2024) documented that the absence of any recognition procedure leaves trans people's identity documents permanently mismatched and exposed to police and institutional mistreatment.  By March 2025, Human Rights Watch counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender recognition and named six — among them Tabasco, the subject of the dedicated 2024 report — whose legislatures had enacted none. For a visible trans visitor the document mismatch is the practical trigger: an ID that does not match presentation invites the questioning and mistreatment the report records.

sources.claim: Tabasco-specific entry: the state has NOT reformed its legislation and has no legal gender recognition procedure - one of EIGHT states with none (record said 'six'; two more states are practice-only). Documented consequence: where no procedure exists, mismatched identity documents invite police stops and institutional mistreatment.

Tabasco-dedicated HRW report (6 Mar 2024, produced with a local community centre for inclusion): Tabasco has no legal gender recognition procedure, so trans people's identity documents never match their gender, curtailing rights across four socio-economic areas. Example: Karina Gómez, a trans woman, murdered in Tabasco in August 2023. For this record: direct on-the-ground documentation of the documentary mismatch that endangers visible trans people in Tabasco itself.

records.name: Tamaulipas
records.current_summary: Tamaulipas is among the six Mexican states whose legislatures have enacted no legal procedure for recognising gender identity, per Human Rights Watch's March 2025 count of 22 of 32 states having legislated one. Where no procedure exists, trans residents' identity documents remain permanently mismatched with any official record of who they are.  The consequences of that absence are documented in the companion 2024 Human Rights Watch report on one such state: mismatched documents invite exactly the police checks and institutional mistreatment that most endanger a visible trans visitor in daily interactions.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time; the underlying source is a Human Rights Watch country overview (31 March 2025) on transgender rights progress and challenges in Mexico, headlining that 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and naming six whose legislatures had enacted none.

HRW's state-by-state table (31 Mar 2025) records that Tamaulipas 'has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people', placing it among the eight Mexican states with no procedure at all, against 22 of 32 states that have legislated an administrative procedure (two more have one in practice only). For a trans person whose documents are issued in Tamaulipas this means there is no administrative route to change identity documents to match their gender identity, which is the record's core claim.

On 18 June 2025 the Tamaulipas state Congress unanimously approved reforms to the local Penal Code adding a chapter on crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression, explicitly banning 'conversion therapies' with prison terms of 2-6 years and fines of up to 2,000 UMA; penalties rise by half when victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or in subordinate settings such as family, medical or workplace. Dated evidence that Tamaulipas's criminal law protects gender identity even though the state still lacks an administrative gender-recognition procedure.

On 4 February 2026 deputies of Tamaulipas's 66th legislature and LGBT+ civil-society groups (including Tamaulipas Diversidad, Vihda Trans A.C., Tendremos Alas A.C. and La Resistencia Trans) agreed a joint agenda to push a Gender Identity Law and anti-discrimination and health reforms, noting the initiatives have been pending since June 2025 and that the absent law keeps limiting trans people's access to health, education and employment. Confirms that as of early 2026 no legal gender-recognition procedure exists in Tamaulipas and a Gender Identity Law remains unpassed.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time; the underlying source is a Human Rights Watch country overview (31 March 2025) on transgender rights progress and challenges in Mexico, headlining that 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and naming six whose legislatures had enacted none.

HRW's March 2025 state-by-state rundown of legal gender recognition records that Tlaxcala's congress passed a 2019 reform to the state Civil Code (Decree D.113, dated 1 October 2019) creating an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, linking the decree text on the state congress's own site. The feature contrasts Tlaxcala with states it lists as still having no procedure, such as Tabasco and Tamaulipas. For this record it states the concrete legal basis a trans visitor would rely on to update documents in Tlaxcala: an administrative route requiring no court proceeding.

The national framework page Tlaxcala stands under: same-sex marriage legal nationwide since 2022 (the final states completed legalisation that year), federal protection against sexual-orientation discrimination since 2003, and — after the Supreme Court's 17 October 2018 ruling — a transgender person can change name and gender marker through a simple administrative procedure based on self-declaration, the page listing administrative legal gender recognition as available in Mexico City and 18 states. The page names Tlaxcala directly: its civil-union law took effect on 12 January 2017. It also notes outed LGBTQ soldiers face severe harassment and are often discharged; a visitor's practical exposure is the national baseline locally enforced.

records.name: Yucatan
records.current_summary: Yucatan is not among the six Mexican states whose legislatures have enacted no legal gender-recognition procedure, per Human Rights Watch's March 2025 count (22 of 32 states have legislated one).  No Yucatan-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern against transgender people is supported by the surviving sources; the national criminal and human-rights framework applies in the state as elsewhere in Mexico.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time; the underlying source is a Human Rights Watch country overview (31 March 2025) on transgender rights progress and challenges in Mexico, headlining that 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and naming six whose legislatures had enacted none.

The national framework page names Yucatán directly: on 1 July 2013 the Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled that two petitioners were able to marry and on 8 August 2013 the first same-sex couple legally married in the state; the Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015 and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022, and Yucatán is listed as enacting a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban on 25 August 2021, still in effect alongside the state bans from Mexico City (31 July 2020) and elsewhere. The page also records the federal framework: same-sex acts decriminalised since 1871, tolerance of sexual diversity documented among Yucatán Maya groups, and the conversion-therapy ban passed federally by the Chamber of Deputies in March 2023 (267-104) after a 69-16 Senate vote in October 2022.

HRW's state-by-state rundown of legal gender recognition (March 2025) carries a dedicated Yucatán entry: 'In 2024, the state's congress passed a reform to the Civil Registry Law to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition', linking to the state's official gazette (Diario Oficial, 26 April 2024, on yucatan.gob.mx). This places Yucatán among the Mexican states with an administrative - rather than court-ordered - route for transgender people to update legal gender, which is the concrete local procedure a trans visitor's document situation turns on; the same feature explains which states lack any procedure.

records.current_summary: Zacatecas is not among the six Mexican states whose legislatures have enacted no legal gender-recognition procedure, per Human Rights Watch's March 2025 count (22 of 32 states have legislated one).  No Zacatecas-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern targeting transgender people appears in the surviving sources; Mexico's national criminal law and gender-recognition regime apply here as elsewhere in the country.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time; the underlying source is a Human Rights Watch country overview (31 March 2025) on transgender rights progress and challenges in Mexico, headlining that 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and naming six whose legislatures had enacted none.

La Jornada Zacatecas, 23 December 2022, reports that with 14 votes in favour and 7 against, deputies of the state's 64th Legislature approved the reform of the Family Code of the State of Zacatecas on gender identity, establishing the possibility of issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community; the Justice Committee had already issued a positive opinion (dictamen) on the reform. This is the local record of the 2022 enactment against which this record's central claim — that Zacatecas is not among the states lacking a legislated gender-recognition procedure — is checked. Page verified via the Wayback Machine snapshot of 7 October 2025; the live ljz.mx URL is Cloudflare-blocked (HTTP 403).

Sopitas, 30 August 2021, reports that on 25 August 2021 the Congress of Zacatecas approved prohibiting and sanctioning conversion therapies or 'ECOSIG' (Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género) by adding fraction VI to article 182 Bis of the state Penal Code — penalised with one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work against anyone who incites hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or promotes such practices; the same session also typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity in the state Penal Code. The article further records that the gender-identity law initiative debated alongside (constitutional and family-code reform) failed to obtain enough votes and remained pending at the time — the reform only passed in December 2022. Documents the protective state-level criminal-law floor applying in Zacatecas, with an explicit ban on practices aimed at changing gender identity.

Human Rights Watch's March 2025 state-by-state feature on legal gender recognition carries a dedicated Zacatecas entry: in 2022 the state congress passed a reform amending the Family Code to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, and in 2023 the director of the state Civil Registry issued guidelines implementing the law, both linked to the official state gazette (periodico.zacatecas.gob.mx). This is the per-state framework source consistent with the record's statement that, in HRW's March 2025 count (22 of 32 states having legislated a procedure at the time), Zacatecas is not among the states lacking one.

records.name: Quebec
records.current_summary: Quebec's recorded profile rests on the national data series: Statistics Canada's March 2026 release on police-reported hate crime (2024 data) shows gender-identity/expression-motivated incidents rising nationally for a fourth consecutive year — +8% to 139, nearly triple 2020 — and identifies no trans-specific provincial pattern for Quebec.  No Quebec-specific anti-trans legislation, ordinance or incident series appears in the surviving sources, alongside national NGO analysis of the same police data; the province's largest city anchors one of the country's most established organised 2SLGBTQ+ communities.

sources.claim: Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026, police-reported hate crime 2024): 4,882 hate crimes reported nationally (+1% on 2023), national rate 12.1 per 100,000 (−2% in 2024, +142% since 2018); provincial rates ranged from 5.3 (Manitoba, Newfoundland and Labrador) to 16.0 (Ontario), with eight provinces stable or declining. No Quebec-specific rate figure appears in the release windows, so it supports the record's national-parity assessment. Federal criminal law and the federal human-rights framework apply uniformly in Quebec.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (redirect to a 27-character stub); the underlying source is Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report, an LGBTIQ+ organisation's analysis of national police hate-crime data including sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations.

CBC News reports (19 June 2025) that Quebec's public security minister announced transgender inmates in the province will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety priorities, in a directive issued just after trans woman Levana Ballouz, convicted of murdering her partner and children, sought a transfer to a women's prison; advocates say the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. This is dated, province-specific evidence of an official Quebec policy change reversing the previous practice of considering gender identity in correctional placement.

Éducaloi reports that on 10 June 2024 Quebec's Human Rights Tribunal found a Montreal bar discriminated against a trans woman in hiring because of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training; the page notes gender identity and expression were added as prohibited grounds of discrimination under Quebec's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms in 2016, and cites 2021 census data that 0.14% of Quebecers aged 15 and older (0.27% of those aged 15-34) identify as transgender. This is Quebec-specific enforcement evidence that trans people can win discrimination claims under provincial law.

IMK's case note on Centre for Gender Advocacy and al. v. Attorney General of Quebec records that after a two-month trial with 29 witnesses the Quebec Superior Court (2021 QCCS 191) declared provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people, that the Court of Appeal largely upheld the decision (2024 QCCA 348), and that the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code. It is a dated, lawyer-verified account of the landmark Quebec court outcome that reshaped the province's rules on sex designation and identity documents.
